newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican companies seen busy in debt markets in '97.
newsitem.headline: Mexican companies seen busy in debt markets in '97.

text.p: Mexican companies are expected to increase international borrowing in 1997, taking advantage of a stable interest rate environment to extend the tenor of their debt, analysts said.
Corporate borrowers are finding that stable interest rates, an improving business scene, and strong demand from foreign investors have helped drive down their borrowing costs.

"The circumstances are such that you have a fairly stable interest rate environment in the U.S. and you have an improved credit scenerio in a lot of Latin countries, so obviously this allows companies to access the markets much easier," Jim Garvey, a corporate analyst at Santander Investment, said.

"Conditions are very favorable. In the United States everything is trading very tight, so in the emerging markets, there are better yielding investment opportunities," said Bankers Trust debt analyst Christopher Taylor.
"On the supply side, Mexican companies learned some very good lessons during the crisis, which is that short-term debt can get you in trouble," he said.

One good example is TV Azteca SA, which in late January placed a two-tranche debt deal. That was a $300 million senior guaranteed note due 2007 to yield 10.5 percent and a $125 million senior guaranteed note to yield 10.15 percent, due 2004.
In early February, Grupo Posadas placed a $50 million five-year bond that had a coupon of 10.375 percent.
Borrowers are turning mainly to the syndicated loan markets or to bonds, although the International Finance Corp has also lent money recently.
Although rumors have speculated that Fomento Economico Mexicano SA (Femsa) may be interested in placing a Eurobond, sources said the company could instead take out a $150 million subordinated loan.
That loan could be over five-years at Libor plus 250 basis points, which would be well under what other top-tier names have been placing their bonds at, analysts said.
There are also rumors that Grupo Embotellador de Mexico, or Gemex, may come to the market with a Yankee bond led by Merrill Lynch.

In the wake of the 1995 financial crisis sparked by the devaluation of the peso in late 1994, the return by Mexican corporate borrowers to debt markets was led by Grupo Televisa SA de CV, Grupo Durango and Cemex SA, analysts said. In May last year, Televisa issued $700 million in a huge debt placement.
In mid-July Cemex made a two-part offering for $600 million.
That was followed later in the month by Grupo Industrial Durango, with its $250 million note that saw strong demand for the paper.
With the loan market more or less limited to about five years, the bond market has become more popular with companies wanting to extend their debt maturities.

"For companies who want to extend their maturities, that (market) is much more reasonable given the longer yield curves in Argentina and Mexico, and they are able to do that," Garvey said. They have been aided in Mexico by the construction of sovereign yield curve by the federal government.
In 1996 Mexican corporate entities issued Eurobonds worth $2.86 billion.
